Certify, Report, or Refuse: Harm-Constrained Conformal Prediction for Clinical Actions

Corresponding author.
Zhiyuan Li Email: zli2562@wisc.edu    Lequan Yu Email: lqyu@hku.hk Affiliation: 1College of Computing & Artificial Intelligence, University of Wisconsin–Madison, Madison, WI, USA
2School of Computing and Data Science, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Abstract

Routing a melanoma case to routine follow-up is a serious action error that diagnostic coverage alone does not rule out. We present Harm-Constrained Risk-Optimal Conformal Prediction (HC-ROCP), a training-free framework that uses frozen classifier probabilities and adds a harm penalty when choosing prediction sets and actions. We test the resulting policies on disjoint calibration splits with multiplicity adjustment. HC-ROCP certifies supported claims, reports descriptive fallback policies, and refuses unsupported subgroup claims. We evaluate these outputs retrospectively on COVID-19 radiographs, ISIC 2019 dermoscopy, and EyePACS-to-APTOS retinopathy transfer. Across ten calibration seeds, HC-ROCP reduces COVID-19 severe-action errors from the exact risk-optimal baseline’s 4.68% to 0.54%. At a 5% budget, global claims are certified for COVID-19 and ISIC, but the rare squamous-cell-carcinoma claim is refused. At 1%, all settings receive descriptive reports. For each budget, we also report the minimum severe-case count needed to pass the global harm gate with zero errors, providing a starting point for further data collection.

keywords
conformal prediction, conformal risk control, clinical decision support, medical imaging

1 Introduction

Medical-image classifiers can inform decisions about routine follow-up, further testing, or specialist referral. A serious error occurs when a severe condition receives an inappropriate action, such as routing melanoma to routine follow-up. Conformal prediction provides sets of possible diagnoses with marginal label-coverage guarantees (Vovk et al., 2005; Shafer and Vovk, 2008). Risk-Optimal Conformal Prediction (ROCP) uses these sets to choose downstream actions under a robust loss criterion (Wang and Dobriban, 2026).

Neither label coverage nor average loss directly controls how often a severe case receives a harmful action. A set may contain the true diagnosis even when the selected action is harmful, and low average loss can conceal errors concentrated in a rare severe class. Low observed error also needs enough data to support a population-level claim. In our ISIC study, for example, zero errors among 42 squamous-cell-carcinoma cases are insufficient to certify an error rate below 5%5\% under our multiplicity correction. We therefore assess severe-action errors separately and test which global and subgroup claims the calibration data support.

Risk-controlling prediction sets, conformal risk control, and learn-then-test provide tools for evaluating prespecified risks (Bates et al., 2021; Angelopoulos et al., 2024a; Angelopoulos et al., 2025). We use these tools to connect two tasks: constructing policies that target severe-action errors and auditing the evidence for their coverage and harm claims. The audit supports three reporting decisions: certify a supported claim, report a descriptive fallback policy, or refuse an unsupported subgroup claim.

We introduce Harm-Constrained Risk-Optimal Conformal Prediction (HC-ROCP), a framework based on frozen classifier probabilities. We extend ROCP’s objective with a penalty for harmful actions, weighted by the predicted probability of a severe label. Varying this penalty and the coverage parameter produces a finite family of policies. Separate calibration splits test their coverage and harm rates with multiplicity adjustment. These tests determine the selected policy’s global evidence label and which subgroup claims are supported. Figure  shows an actual output. Section 3 explains these labels before introducing the optimization.

We evaluate the method retrospectively in three imaging settings. On COVID-19, severe-action error is roughly ninefold lower than exact ROCP across ten calibration seeds, at higher modeled loss. ISIC tests whether aggregate evidence also supports a rare-subgroup claim. EyePACS-to-APTOS examines recalibration after a domain shift with few severe cases. No setting certifies at 1%1\%. We vary the budget to identify which claims can pass and calculate the severe-case counts needed even with zero observed errors.

The paper makes three contributions:

  • •

    We extend ROCP with a penalty for prespecified severe-action errors, targeting them during the construction of prediction sets and actions (Section 4).

  • •

    We jointly test coverage and harm when selecting a policy, report descriptive fallbacks, and withhold unsupported subgroup claims (Sections 4.3 and 5).

  • •

    We measure how subgroup size and candidate multiplicity affect certification, and how costs and referral options change the available policies (Section 7).

2 Related Work

Coverage and Risk Control.

Split conformal prediction controls marginal label coverage under exchangeability (Vovk et al., 2005; Shafer and Vovk, 2008). Risk-controlling prediction sets extend the target to losses (Bates et al., 2021), while conformal risk control and learn-then-test provide general tools for risk calibration and testing (Angelopoulos et al., 2024a; Angelopoulos et al., 2025). These tools can evaluate many kinds of decision policies. Our contribution integrates these bounds with harm-aware set/action construction and explicit global/subgroup reporting.

Decisions from Prediction Sets.

ROCP optimizes a prediction set and its downstream action under a robust loss criterion (Wang and Dobriban, 2026). HC-ROCP preserves this action rule but adds a penalty for harmful actions on severe cases and tests their frequency alongside coverage. Conformal decision theory and utility-directed conformal prediction also connect uncertainty to decisions and utilities (Lekeufack et al., 2024; Cortes-Gomez et al., 2025). Conformal triage separates cases into high-risk, low-risk, and uncertain groups, with predictive-value guarantees for the first two (Angelopoulos et al., 2024b). Action-conditional conformal prediction defines risk conditional on the action taken (Zhu et al., 2026). We instead measure harmful-action frequency among cases whose true labels belong to the prespecified severe classes.

Joint Tests and Evidence Reporting.

Related work studies joint certification across candidate policies (Yu and Liu, 2026) and hierarchical group-conditional control (Salem et al., 2026). Gurram (2026) distinguishes average-risk statements from high-confidence guarantees. Liu et al. (2026) study joint certification of error among accepted answers and a minimum answer rate under bounded-ratio covariate shift. Their procedure returns a refusal when no candidate passes both tests. HC-ROCP instead tests diagnostic label coverage and harmful-action frequency among severe cases over a finite, potentially non-nested policy family. We report global and subgroup evidence separately and retain descriptive fallbacks when joint certification fails.

3 Problem and Outputs

The Decision Problem.

An image XX has label Y∈{1,…,K}Y\in\{1,\ldots,K\} and frozen classifier probabilities p(⋅∣X)p(\cdot\mid X) (notation: Appendix A). Before calibration, we specify actions 𝒜\mathcal{A}, a loss matrix Λ\Lambda, severe labels YHY_{H}, and harmful actions AHA_{H}. A policy π\pi returns a nonempty set Sπ​(X)S_{\pi}(X) and action aπ​(Sπ​(X))a_{\pi}(S_{\pi}(X)). The severe-action-error event is

H=𝟏​{Y∈YH,aπ​(Sπ​(X))∈AH}.H=\mathbf{1}\{Y\in Y_{H},\ a_{\pi}(S_{\pi}(X))\in A_{H}\}.

We require coverage cov⁡(π)=P⁡(Y∈Sπ​(X))≥1−α\mathrm{cov}(\pi)=P(Y\in S_{\pi}(X))\geq 1-\alpha and conditional error

RH​(π)=P⁡(aπ​(Sπ​(X))∈AH∣Y∈YH)≤δ.R_{H}(\pi)=P(a_{\pi}(S_{\pi}(X))\in A_{H}\mid Y\in Y_{H})\leq\delta.

The denominator contains only severe cases. Modeled loss is ℒ⁡(π)=𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(aπ​(Sπ​(X)),Y)]\mathcal{L}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}[\ell(a_{\pi}(S_{\pi}(X)),Y)], using Λ\Lambda to express relative action preferences.

Evidence Labels.

A gate tests a requested claim against the available calibration evidence (Table ). HC-ROCP certifies a policy when coverage and all-severe harm gates pass together. Otherwise, it reports a fallback policy with its descriptive evidence level. Each subgroup claim receives its own harm test: passing supports certification, and failing produces a refusal. Disease-defined subgroup membership is determined from retrospective reference labels.

A Running Example.

For the melanoma image in Figure , the selected ISIC policy returns {MEL,SCC}\{\mathrm{MEL},\mathrm{SCC}\} and the urgent specialist pathway. The policy carries an expected-risk descriptive label, and the MEL subgroup’s insufficient label records refusal of its requested claim. The global label applies to the policy; the subgroup label applies to the MEL population. ISIC sets are larger on average (Section 7.5).

4 HC-ROCP: Construction and Audit

We first construct a set/action family, then audit it on separate data (Figure ; Algorithm C).

4.1 From a Prediction Set to an Action

We retain ROCP’s robust action rule. Let ℓin​(a,S)\ell_{\rm in}(a;S) and ℓout​(a,S)\ell_{\rm out}(a;S) be the largest losses inside and outside SS, setting ℓout=ℓin\ell_{\rm out}=\ell_{\rm in} when the outside is empty. The robust risk is

ρ⁡(S)=mina∈𝒜⁡[ℓin​(a,S)+αact​{ℓout​(a,S)−ℓin​(a,S)}+].\rho(S)=\min_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\!\left[\ell_{\rm in}(a;S)+\alpha_{\mathrm{act}}\{\ell_{\rm out}(a;S)-\ell_{\rm in}(a;S)\}_{+}\right].

It bounds worst-case expected loss when at most αact\alpha_{\mathrm{act}} mass lies outside SS (Wang and Dobriban, 2026). The minimizing action is a⁡(S)a(S), with fixed-order tie-breaking. Here αact\alpha_{\mathrm{act}} defines the action rule, while α\alpha defines the audited coverage target. ROCP balances this risk against p⁡(S∣x)=∑y∈Sp⁡(y∣x)p(S\mid x)=\sum_{y\in S}p(y\mid x):

Sβ​(x)∈arg⁡minS≠∅​{ρ⁡(S)−β​p​(S∣x)}.S_{\beta}(x)\in\arg\min_{S\neq\emptyset}\{\rho(S)-\beta p(S\mid x)\}.

4.2 Constructing Harm-Aware Policies

HC-ROCP selects a set minimizing

ρ(S)−βp(S∣x)+γp(YH∣x)𝟏{a(S)∈AH}.\rho(S)-\beta p(S\mid x)+\gamma p(Y_{H}\mid x)\mathbf{1}\{a(S)\in A_{H}\}.

The added term targets harmful actions on inputs assigned high severe-class probability. Its indicator activates only for sets whose robust action lies in AHA_{H}, while p⁡(YH∣x)p(Y_{H}\mid x) weights that penalty by the classifier’s evidence of severity. The action map stays fixed and γ=0\gamma=0 recovers exact ROCP.

The two parameters act through the same set choice. Increasing β\beta rewards probability mass; increasing γ\gamma favors sets whose associated action avoids AHA_{H} on likely severe cases. A change in the preferred action can therefore change which labels enter the set. Jointly varying the parameters searches this coverage/action trade-off (Section 7.6). We enumerate all nonempty subsets in the small label spaces studied here.

This objective generates candidates for

minπ⁡ℒ⁡(π)s.t.cov⁡(π)≥1−α,RH​(π)≤δ.\min_{\pi}\ \mathcal{L}(\pi)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\mathrm{cov}(\pi)\geq 1-\alpha,\ \ R_{H}(\pi)\leq\delta.

Equation (1) is a pointwise, Lagrangian-inspired surrogate for (2); the audit in Section 4.3 tests the population constraints. Joint changes to the set and action produce a potentially non-nested family. We use a construct split to fix the finite candidate family ℱ\mathcal{F} before auditing.

4.3 Joint Testing and Selection

For each candidate, we test whether coverage meets its target and severe-action error stays within budget. On a separate coverage split, Kcov​(π)K_{\rm cov}(\pi) of ncovn_{\rm cov} labels fall inside the set. On the safety split, KH,g​(π)K_{H,g}(\pi) of nH,gn_{H,g} severe cases receive harmful actions in group gg; group 00 includes all severe labels.

For M=|ℱ|M=|\mathcal{F}| policies and GG safety groups including group 00, each test receives η=ε/[M⁡(1+G)]\eta=\varepsilon/[M(1+G)]. One-sided Clopper–Pearson tests produce coverage lower value LcovL_{\rm cov} and harm upper values UH,gU_{H,g}. A policy receives global certification if and only if

Lcov​(π)≥1−αandUH,0​(π)≤δ.L_{\rm cov}(\pi)\geq 1-\alpha\quad\text{and}\quad U_{H,0}(\pi)\leq\delta.

These gates are binomial-exact for a single class and conservative for stratified mixtures under Section 5’s conditions. Among passing policies, we minimize safety-split loss. Simultaneous testing permits this selection on the safety data; utility itself receives no guarantee.

We use the construct split to propose parameter pairs or screen a shortlist, then freeze the family before inspecting coverage or safety outcomes. Because the simultaneous bounds cover every retained candidate, we can select any policy within that family. Adding candidates after inspecting failed gates would require a new validity argument. We use held-out test data to summarize the selected policy’s performance. Only the calibration gates determine which certificate to issue.

4.4 Descriptive Fallbacks and Subgroup Claims

If no policy certifies, the expected-risk fallback requires

Kcov+1ncov+1≥1−α,KH,0+1nH,0+1≤δ.\frac{K_{\rm cov}+1}{n_{\rm cov}+1}\geq 1-\alpha,\qquad\frac{K_{H,0}+1}{n_{H,0}+1}\leq\delta.

If none qualifies, the empirical fallback uses raw proportions. Both select the lowest-loss eligible policy. If neither is feasible, a diagnostic policy minimizes coverage shortfall, empirical harm, then loss. Empty severe groups cannot pass.

Both fallbacks are descriptive (Proposition 2). Each subgroup’s adjusted harm gate determines its own certification status, regardless of the global label.

5 What the Certificate Guarantees

A certificate controls false claims across the tested family for a fixed decision specification. Under the conditions below, with probability at least 1−ε1-\varepsilon over calibration, every certified harm claim meets its requested budget. The two quantities have distinct roles: ε\varepsilon controls the probability of issuing a false claim, while δ\delta bounds the action-error frequency among severe cases. Proofs are in Appendix B.

We condition on the construct split so that the candidate family is fixed, and on the class counts produced by stratified splitting. Observations are i.i.d. within each class, but error probabilities can differ across classes. Accordingly, covw\mathrm{cov}_{w} and RH,g,wR_{H,g,w} average class-conditional coverage and harm using the realized certification-split proportions (Appendix B).

For a single-class subgroup, the count is binomial. For a global mixture, we use the tail comparison below to justify gates computed from the binomial-reference Clopper–Pearson values CPL\mathrm{CP}_{L} and CPU\mathrm{CP}_{U}. The M⁡(1+G)M(1+G) correction accounts for one coverage test and GG safety tests for each of the MM policies.

Theorem 1 (Joint finite-sample certification).

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} have size MM and be fixed without inspecting certification outcomes, conditional on the realized class counts. For each policy and group, form the Clopper–Pearson gate values LcovL_{\rm cov} and UH,gU_{H,g} with η=ε/[M⁡(1+G)]\eta=\varepsilon/[M(1+G)]. Assume every nonempty binomial-reference gate cutoff lies at least one count beyond its null mean, as formalized in Lemma 4. Then, with probability at least 1−ε1-\varepsilon, simultaneously over ℱ\mathcal{F}, passing Lcov​(π)≥1−αL_{\rm cov}(\pi)\geq 1-\alpha implies covw​(π)≥1−α\mathrm{cov}_{w}(\pi)\geq 1-\alpha, and passing UH,g​(π)≤δgU_{H,g}(\pi)\leq\delta_{g} implies RH,g,w​(π)≤δgR_{H,g,w}(\pi)\leq\delta_{g} for every group gg. Thus selection preserves the global statements and every separately passing subgroup statement.

Empirical Check.

Gate-cutoff checks confirm the separation condition throughout (Appendix B); Appendix G gives a simplified simulation of global harm tests.

Proof Sketch.

Conditional on class counts, a global count is a sum of classwise binomials. Under the stated separation, Hoeffding’s comparison bounds its gate tail by the binomial tail with the same mean (Hoeffding, 1956); Clopper–Pearson inversion and a union bound over M⁡(1+G)M(1+G) gates complete the result.

Proposition 2 (Add-one estimate).

Conditional on fixed stratified class counts, let π\pi be fixed without inspecting safety outcomes and write KH=∑i=1nHZiK_{H}=\sum_{i=1}^{n_{H}}Z_{i}, where the ZiZ_{i} are independent Bernoulli variables with possibly different probabilities pip_{i}. For pw=nH−1​∑ipi=RH,0,w​(π)p_{w}=n_{H}^{-1}\sum_{i}p_{i}=R_{H,0,w}(\pi),

𝔼⁡[KH+1nH+1]=nH​pw+1nH+1≥pw.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{K_{H}+1}{n_{H}+1}\right]=\frac{n_{H}p_{w}+1}{n_{H}+1}\geq p_{w}.

The analogous identity holds for coverage indicators and covw​(π)\mathrm{cov}_{w}(\pi). Thus both add-one estimates are upward biased for a fixed policy, but neither is a conditional bound after observing its count or selecting π\pi from ℱ\mathcal{F}.

Proof Sketch.

Since 𝔼⁡[KH]=∑ipi=nH​pw\mathbb{E}[K_{H}]=\sum_{i}p_{i}=n_{H}p_{w}, the displayed identity follows by linearity of expectation; identical reasoning applies to coverage. The expectation is taken before observing the count for the fixed policy.

Theorem 3 (Subgroup certify-or-fallback).

Under the multiplicity correction of Theorem 1 applied to the global group and every requested subgroup, on the simultaneous-validity event: (i) every subgroup gg with UH,g​(π∗)≤δgU_{H,g}(\pi^{*})\leq\delta_{g} is certified; (ii) a subgroup that fails the gate receives no subgroup certificate and the separately certified global policy remains valid (fallback); (iii) the realized risk of a failed subgroup is never claimed to be at most δg\delta_{g}.

Proof Sketch.

Apply Theorem 1 with groups equal to the global group plus all requested subgroups. The simultaneous event includes the global statement and every passing subgroup statement, so withholding a failed subgroup claim preserves the certified global statement.

Choice of Bound.

The binomial-reference bound is useful in the rare-event regime: for SCC’s 42 cases with zero errors and η≈3.7×10−5\eta\approx 3.7\times 10^{-5}, its upper value is 21.6%21.6\%, compared with 34.8%34.8\% for Hoeffding and 62.0%62.0\% for empirical-Bernstein at the same test level.

6 Experimental Setup

Datasets and Decisions.

We evaluate retrospective, single-stage policies against observed disease labels. COVID-19 radiographs (Chowdhury et al., 2020; Rahman et al., 2021) test the action-error/loss trade-off: the three abnormal labels are severe, and taking no action on these cases is harmful. ISIC 2019 dermoscopy (Codella et al., 2019; Tschandl et al., 2018; Hernández-Pérez et al., 2024) tests rare-subgroup evidence: MEL and SCC are severe, and routine follow-up is harmful. EyePACS-to-APTOS retinopathy transfer (EyePACS and California Healthcare Foundation, 2015; Asia Pacific Tele-Ophthalmology Society (APTOS), 2019) tests target-domain recalibration: the two highest grades are severe, and routine rescreen is harmful. Action sets and expert-specified loss matrices appear in Appendix C; partitions are in Table .

Models and Calibration.

All classifiers use ConvNeXt V2-Tiny (Woo et al., 2023) and are frozen before HC-ROCP calibration, which requires no further classifier training. Class-stratified assignment produces disjoint construct, coverage, and safety splits. We set αact=α=0.05\alpha_{\mathrm{act}}=\alpha=0.05, family-wise error allowance ε=0.05\varepsilon=0.05, and reference budgets δ∈{1%,2%,5%}\delta\in\{1\%,2\%,5\%\}. Five clinicians contributed to the decision specifications and endorsed these budgets as reference points (Appendix C).

Candidate β\beta values target coverage 0.950.95, 0.9750.975, and 0.990.99, crossed with the γ\gamma grid. The higher targets provide room for finite-sample uncertainty, so joint selection can yield coverage above the required 0.950.95.

Interpreting the Costs.

The loss matrices encode relative preferences among available actions. For MEL, costs of 1010, 44, 11, and 00 rank routine follow-up, dermatology referral, biopsy workup, and the urgent specialist pathway. We define the severe-action-error event separately from these costs, so we can vary the costs without changing which errors we count.

Comparisons and Metrics.

Exact ROCP uses the same subset enumeration with γ=0\gamma=0; the original release solver uses a different threshold-based implementation (Wang and Dobriban, 2026). We also compare RAC, APS, RAPS, SAPS, Mondrian APS, LAS, SOCOP, utility-directed CP, Bayes action, always-safe action, and CRC/LTT action adapters (Kiyani et al., 2025; Romano et al., 2020; Angelopoulos et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2024; Vovk, 2013; Sadinle et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2026; Cortes-Gomez et al., 2025). Appendix C documents official-code and formula adapters; action-only methods have no set coverage.

All methods share frozen probabilities, losses, and test observations. Tables  and  compare full protocols (calibration details in Appendix E). Table  summarizes ten-seed baseline comparisons; Table  compares protocol variants on the reference split. We report coverage, mean modeled loss, severe-action-error rate, and evidence labels. Ten-seed means and sample standard deviations quantify calibration-partition variation on fixed test sets. Table , budget sweeps, and subgroup counts use one reference split. Paired tests are detailed in Appendix E; 500 nested-bootstrap repetitions are described in Appendix F.

7 Results

Three findings organize the results: HC-ROCP reduces severe-action error at a modeled-loss cost; global and subgroup audits support different claims; and budget, severe-case counts, and candidate multiplicity determine the evidence required for certification.

7.1 COVID-19: Lower Error at Higher Modeled Loss

Across ten seeds, HC-ROCP reduces severe-action error from exact ROCP’s 4.68%4.68\% to 0.54%0.54\%, while loss increases from 0.3910.391 to 1.1811.181. This approximately 8.78.7-fold error reduction costs less than always taking the safe action, whose loss is 2.9352.935.

The reference policy has test harm 0.50%0.50\% and loss 1.0801.080 (Figure ). Its adjusted safety upper bound is 4.69%4.69\% from 366 severe cases, yielding an expected-risk report at 1%1\%. The official CRC action adapter reaches 0.14%0.14\% harm at loss 1.5341.534 on this split; it reports an action-only output (Figure ).

7.2 ISIC: Aggregate Evidence Leaves SCC Unsupported

On ISIC, the reference policy has test harm 0.87%0.87\% and an expected-risk label at the 1%1\% budget. The subgroup bounds are much wider. MEL has 302 safety cases and an upper bound of 4.88%4.88\%, compared with 21.56%21.56\% for SCC’s 42 cases. Neither subgroup passes at 1%1\%. At 5%5\%, the global and MEL claims pass, but the SCC claim is still refused (Figure ; all subgroups in Figure ).

Ten-seed mean harm falls from exact ROCP’s 1.84%1.84\% to 0.66%0.66\%. The release solver has numerically lower harm and loss at different coverage; Appendix E reports the paired comparisons. The 5%5\% certified ISIC policy selects γ=0\gamma=0, with test coverage 0.97660.9766, harm 0.47%0.47\%, and loss 1.6311.631.

7.3 EyePACS to APTOS: Zero Errors, Limited Evidence

On EyePACS-to-APTOS, all methods have zero test harm. HC-ROCP selects γ=0\gamma=0, with ten-seed mean loss 1.7051.705 versus exact ROCP’s 1.5141.514. The joint search includes γ=0\gamma=0, allowing it to retain an unpenalized policy. We also observe zero safety errors for the selected reference policy, but this is based on only 65 severe cases. At its adjusted test level η\eta, the upper bound is 1−η1/65=13.22%1-\eta^{1/65}=13.22\%, well above the 1%1\% budget. The policy receives an empirical fallback label (Table ).

7.4 Budgets and Evidence Requirements

For COVID-19, we select the same policy at the 1%1\% and 5%5\% budgets. Its calibration bound passes only the latter. In this sweep, global claims are certified for COVID-19 and ISIC only at 5%5\%. EyePACS-to-APTOS returns descriptive reports at all three budgets (Figure ).

The zero-error case gives an optimistic sample requirement. For zero errors among nHn_{H} severe cases, the binomial-reference upper value is 1−η1/nH1-\eta^{1/n_{H}}. The minimum count for this gate to meet a budget δ\delta is

n0=⌈log⁡ηlog⁡(1−δ)⌉.n_{0}=\left\lceil\frac{\log\eta}{\log(1-\delta)}\right\rceil.

Table  evaluates this threshold under the reference full-family Bonferroni correction. At 1%1\%, all three settings have fewer severe cases than this zero-error threshold. Nonzero errors and the separate coverage and subgroup gates impose further requirements.

A construct-only shortlist lowers COVID-19’s zero-error requirement from 1,233 cases for the full family to 459 for one candidate with the same coverage and subgroup claims. Both exceed the available 366 cases (Table ). Aggressive screening can also discard a policy that performs better on the disjoint safety split.

Figure (a) combines synthetic single-policy power curves with a separate post-selection count diagnostic on real COVID-19 severe cases. The real-data series yields zero gate passes; its sampling procedure is described in Appendix F.

The official LTT action adapter likewise certifies zero policies at 1%1\%, then certifies 16 COVID-19 and 7 ISIC candidates at 5%5\% (Table ).

7.5 Set Size, Costs, and Referral

Set Size.

Set size counts the diagnosis labels returned for an image. We use these sets primarily to choose actions. Mean sizes across ten seeds are 1.732±0.1851.732\pm 0.185 of four labels for COVID-19, 6.172±0.4046.172\pm 0.404 of eight for ISIC, and 4.351±0.1394.351\pm 0.139 of five for retinopathy. Each exceeds exact ROCP’s mean (Table ), quantifying the set-size cost alongside coverage.

Cost Scale.

We halve the costs assigned to harmful actions on severe COVID-19 cases and repeat the full procedure. No empirically feasible candidate remains in any of the ten seeds, and the diagnostic fallbacks have harm 3.05%±0.41%3.05\%\pm 0.41\% (Figure ). With the original and doubled costs, harm is 0.54%±0.32%0.54\%\pm 0.32\% and 0.55%±0.32%0.55\%\pm 0.32\%, respectively. Both retain expected-risk labels.

Referral.

We add a referral action, modeled as non-harmful, and vary its cost. On the reference split, modeled loss falls from 1.0801.080 to 0.280.28–0.400.40. At the lowest cost, however, the policy refers every case (Appendix H). We report referral rates alongside loss to distinguish selective referral from referring every case.

7.6 Why Joint Selection Matters

The fixed-β\beta diagnostic loses coverage: calibrating β\beta on the construct split at γ=0\gamma=0 and then choosing γ\gamma by a safety-count rule gives 78.6%78.6\% test coverage, versus 99.0%99.0\% under joint selection (Appendix F).

Nested bootstrap retains each dataset’s original global evidence label in all 500 repetitions while the selected parameters vary.

8 Discussion and Limitations

Certify, Report, and Refuse.

Across the three datasets, we obtain global certificates for COVID-19 and ISIC at 5%5\% and descriptive reports for all settings at 1%1\%. The SCC subgroup claim remains unsupported even when ISIC’s global claim passes. We report observed performance for all selected policies, including those whose requested claims fail the certification tests.

Testing more candidate policies increases the multiplicity correction and raises the zero-error sample requirement. Costs and available actions instead change which policies are constructed. Future work will compare frozen classifiers under matched decision specifications and calibration budgets, improve construct-only screening, and develop reassessment procedures for workflow changes. The same certification tests can be applied to other prespecified policy families with appropriate selection control.

Path to Clinical Evaluation.

Local clinicians would specify actions, harmful events, costs, and acceptable budgets, followed by auditing on representative labeled data. A prospective silent-mode study could assess action errors, subgroup evidence, and projected referral volume before recommendations enter care. An approved clinician-supervised study would subsequently evaluate overrides, escalation delays, workload, and patient outcomes. Hospital-specific review would also determine whether available referral capacity supports the modeled policies.

Limitations.

First, we evaluate modeled actions against retrospective labels. The results therefore say nothing about actual patient outcomes or clinician workload. Expert-specified costs have not been validated as clinical utilities. The single-stage models omit treatment sequences, capacity constraints, and overrides, and COVID-19 actions may co-occur.

Second, calibration seeds share classifiers and test observations. Validity requires within-class i.i.d. sampling and the gate-cutoff conditions of Section 5, and targets the realized calibration mixtures. Changes in prevalence or workflow require reassessment.

Third, the objective has no cardinality penalty, so large prediction sets can limit diagnostic specificity. Exact enumeration scales exponentially with label count, and robustness across classifier backbones remains to be evaluated.

9 Conclusion

We presented HC-ROCP, which constructs prediction sets and actions to target severe-action errors and tests the evidence for global and subgroup claims. Across three imaging settings, global claims are certified for COVID-19 and ISIC at 5%5\%, but SCC remains unsupported and all settings return descriptive reports at 1%1\%. Under the full-family correction, even zero observed errors would require more severe cases than are available at 1%1\%, giving practitioners a concrete starting point for further data collection.

Clopper–Pearson Bounds.

For K∼Binomial⁡(n,p)K\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(n,p), the exact one-sided lower bound

CPL​(k,n,η)=inf{p:Prp⁡(Bin⁡(n,p)≥k)≥η}\mathrm{CP}_{L}(k,n,\eta)=\inf\{p:\Pr_{p}(\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)\geq k)\geq\eta\}

equals the η\eta-quantile of the Beta distribution Beta⁡(k,n−k+1)\mathrm{Beta}(k,n-k+1) (for k≥1k\geq 1, and 00 otherwise), and satisfies Pr⁡(p≥CPL)≥1−η\Pr(p\geq\mathrm{CP}_{L})\geq 1-\eta. The exact upper bound

CPU​(k,n,η)=sup{p:Prp⁡(Bin⁡(n,p)≤k)≥η}\mathrm{CP}_{U}(k,n,\eta)=\sup\{p:\Pr_{p}(\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)\leq k)\geq\eta\}

equals the (1−η)(1-\eta)-quantile of Beta⁡(k+1,n−k)\mathrm{Beta}(k+1,n-k) (for k<nk<n, and 11 otherwise), and satisfies Pr⁡(p≤CPU)≥1−η\Pr(p\leq\mathrm{CP}_{U})\geq 1-\eta.

Let ncov,yn_{{\rm cov},y} be the fixed number of coverage-split observations with label yy, and let nH,g,yn_{H,g,y} be the fixed number of safety-split observations from severe class yy in group gg. The conditional targets are

covw​(π)=∑yncov,yncov​Pr⁡(Y∈Sπ​(X)∣Y=y),\mathrm{cov}_{w}(\pi)=\sum_{y}\frac{n_{{\rm cov},y}}{n_{\rm cov}}\Pr(Y\in S_{\pi}(X)\mid Y=y),

For a binomial-reference coverage target qq and harm target rr, define

kη​(n,q)=min⁡{k:CPL​(k,n,η)≥q},cη​(n,r)=max⁡{k:CPU​(k,n,η)≤r}.k_{\eta}(n,q)=\min\{k:\mathrm{CP}_{L}(k,n,\eta)\geq q\},\qquad c_{\eta}(n,r)=\max\{k:\mathrm{CP}_{U}(k,n,\eta)\leq r\}.

Lemma 4 (Poisson–binomial tail comparison).

Let Z1,…,ZnZ_{1},\ldots,Z_{n} be independent Bernoulli variables with means p1,…,pnp_{1},\ldots,p_{n}, let K=∑iZiK=\sum_{i}Z_{i}, and let p¯=n−1​∑ipi\bar{p}=n^{-1}\sum_{i}p_{i}. For an integer k≥n​p¯+1k\geq n\bar{p}+1,

Pr(K≥k)≤Pr{Binomial(n,p¯)≥k};\Pr(K\geq k)\leq\Pr\{\mathrm{Binomial}(n,\bar{p})\geq k\};

for an integer c≤n​p¯−1c\leq n\bar{p}-1,

Pr(K≤c)≤Pr{Binomial(n,p¯)≤c}.\Pr(K\leq c)\leq\Pr\{\mathrm{Binomial}(n,\bar{p})\leq c\}.

These are the separated-tail comparisons of Hoeffding (1956); the one-count conditions are essential. Pr{Lcov(π)≥q}≤Pr{Bin(ncov,covw(π))≥kη}≤Pr{Bin(ncov,q)≥kη}≤η.\Pr\{L_{\rm cov}(\pi)\geq q\}\leq\Pr\{\mathrm{Bin}(n_{\rm cov},\mathrm{cov}_{w}(\pi))\geq k_{\eta}\}\leq\Pr\{\mathrm{Bin}(n_{\rm cov},q)\geq k_{\eta}\}\leq\eta.

If RH,g,w​(π)>δgR_{H,g,w}(\pi)>\delta_{g}, the second cutoff condition, Lemma 4, lower-tail monotonicity, and CPU\mathrm{CP}_{U} inversion yield

For a single-class subgroup, the corresponding Poisson–binomial distribution is binomial and the comparison is equality. Direct evaluation of the integer cutoffs verifies the separation conditions for every setting evaluated under Theorem 1; the largest per-test error is 0.010.01. Each of the M⁡(1+G)M(1+G) false-passing events has probability at most η=ε/[M⁡(1+G)]\eta=\varepsilon/[M(1+G)]; a union bound gives

Hence, with probability at least 1−ε1-\varepsilon, every passing coverage or group-safety gate supports its corresponding design-weighted criterion. Because this event is simultaneous over the candidate family, selecting π∗\pi^{*} by certification-split utility leaves the global and separately passing subgroup statements intact; utility itself receives no guarantee.

Proof of Proposition 2.

Conditional on the stratified counts, fix π\pi without inspecting the safety outcomes. Independence and linearity give 𝔼⁡[KH]=∑ipi=nH​pw\mathbb{E}[K_{H}]=\sum_{i}p_{i}=n_{H}p_{w}. Therefore

Replacing the harm indicators by coverage indicators gives the same identity with pw=covw​(π)p_{w}=\mathrm{cov}_{w}(\pi).

Proof of Theorem 3.

Run the construction of Theorem 1 with the safety groups equal to {global}∪{requested subgroups}\{\text{global}\}\cup\{\text{requested subgroups}\}, so G=1+|subgroups|G=1+|\text{subgroups}| and the per-test error is ε/[M⁡(1+G)]\varepsilon/[M(1+G)]. On the simultaneous gate-validity event, UH,g​(π∗)≤δgU_{H,g}(\pi^{*})\leq\delta_{g} implies RH,g,w​(π∗)≤δgR_{H,g,w}(\pi^{*})\leq\delta_{g}. If a subgroup fails the gate, the algorithm withholds its certificate and reports the global status; the global design-weighted coverage and safety statements hold on the same event regardless of the subgroup decisions. No statement about RH,g,w​(π∗)R_{H,g,w}(\pi^{*}) is made for a refused subgroup.

Appendix C Implementation Details

Action Sets and Loss Matrices

Five clinical experts designed the action categories and severe-action-error definitions: two dermatologists for ISIC, two ophthalmologists for EyePACS–APTOS, and one respiratory-medicine clinician for COVID-19. These experts specified the loss matrices for their respective tasks and confirmed the final entries shown in Table .

The escalation ordering is informed by NICE NG12 and dermatology guidance for skin lesions (National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, 2015), and AAO guidance for retinopathy (American Academy of Ophthalmology, 2024). The primary 1%1\% budget was motivated as a cross-domain reference by chest-pain risk tolerances (Than et al., 2013) and the ACEP policy’s 30-day MACE framing (Tomaszewski et al., 2018).

COVID-19 actions are informed by WHO management guidance (World Health Organization, 2020).

ℱfeas←{π:Lcov(π)≥1−α,UH,0(π)≤δ}\mathcal{F}_{\rm feas}\leftarrow\{\pi:L_{\rm cov}(\pi)\geq 1-\alpha,\ U_{H,0}(\pi)\leq\delta\}  ℱexp←{π:(Kcov(π)+1)/(ncov+1)≥1−α,(KH,0(π)+1)/(nH,0+1)≤δ}\mathcal{F}_{\rm exp}\leftarrow\{\pi:(K_{\rm cov}(\pi)+1)/(n_{\rm cov}+1)\geq 1-\alpha,\ (K_{H,0}(\pi)+1)/(n_{H,0}+1)\leq\delta\}  ℱemp←{π:Kcov(π)/ncov≥1−α,R^H,0(π)≤δ}\mathcal{F}_{\rm emp}\leftarrow\{\pi:K_{\rm cov}(\pi)/n_{\rm cov}\geq 1-\alpha,\ \widehat{R}_{H,0}(\pi)\leq\delta\}  \eIfℱfeas≠∅\mathcal{F}_{\rm feas}\neq\emptyset π∗←arg⁡minπ∈ℱfeas​loss𝒟safety​(π)\pi^{*}\leftarrow\arg\min_{\pi\in\mathcal{F}_{\rm feas}}\mathrm{loss}_{\mathcal{D}_{\rm safety}}(\pi)  level ←\leftarrow high-confidence  \eIfℱexp≠∅\mathcal{F}_{\rm exp}\neq\emptyset π∗←arg⁡minπ∈ℱexp​loss𝒟safety​(π)\pi^{*}\leftarrow\arg\min_{\pi\in\mathcal{F}_{\rm exp}}\mathrm{loss}_{\mathcal{D}_{\rm safety}}(\pi)  level ←\leftarrow expected-risk  \eIfℱemp≠∅\mathcal{F}_{\rm emp}\neq\emptyset π∗←arg⁡minπ∈ℱemp​loss𝒟safety​(π)\pi^{*}\leftarrow\arg\min_{\pi\in\mathcal{F}_{\rm emp}}\mathrm{loss}_{\mathcal{D}_{\rm safety}}(\pi)  level ←\leftarrow empirical  π∗←arg⁡minπ∈ℱ​[max⁡(0, 1−α−Kcov​(π)/ncov),R^H,0​(π),loss𝒟safety​(π)]\pi^{*}\leftarrow\arg\min_{\pi\in\mathcal{F}}\bigl[\max(0,\,1-\alpha-K_{\rm cov}(\pi)/n_{\rm cov}),\ \widehat{R}_{H,0}(\pi),\ \mathrm{loss}_{\mathcal{D}_{\rm safety}}(\pi)\bigr]  level ←\leftarrow infeasible fallback  \ForEachsubgroup gg status(gg) ←\leftarrow certified if UH,g​(π∗)≤δgU_{H,g}(\pi^{*})\leq\delta_{g}, else insufficient 

We allocate one third of calibration observations to each of the construct, coverage, and safety splits, using stratified assignment. The β\beta grid is obtained by coverage calibration at targets {0.95,0.975,0.99}\{0.95,0.975,0.99\} crossed with a log-spaced γ\gamma grid, yielding M=2394M=2394 (COVID-19), 336336 (ISIC 2019), and 126126 (EyePACS–APTOS) candidates. Randomized RAPS/SAPS baselines use independent fixed random streams for calibration and test.

Baseline Implementations.

We use the authors’ released implementations of ROCP, RAPS, SOCOP, CRC, and LTT with the same frozen classifier probabilities. For ROCP’s reference-split comparison, a single global β\beta is fitted by bisection to 95%95\% empirical coverage on the full calibration split. The exact, matched ROCP variant instead enumerates every nonempty label subset and is the γ=0\gamma=0 member of our family.

RAPS uses a randomized score with kreg=1k_{\rm reg}=1 and λ=0.01\lambda=0.01, and SOCOP uses λ=0.0625\lambda=0.0625. CRC applies its published calibration rule to the monotone action family; LTT uses Hoeffding–Bentkus pp-values with Bonferroni correction. SAPS implements the published randomized scoring formula. Utility-directed CP uses the score-3 adapter distributed with ROCP.

Classifiers and Preprocessing.

All classifiers are ConvNeXt V2-Tiny backbones (Woo et al., 2023) initialized from ImageNet-22k pre-trained weights and fine-tuned per dataset (Table ). Images are resized to 224×224224\times 224 and normalized with ImageNet statistics; training uses random resized crops, horizontal/vertical flips, and color jitter, while validation and test use a 256256-resize followed by a center crop. Models are optimized with AdamW under a cosine learning-rate schedule, early stopping on validation balanced accuracy, and cross-entropy loss with label smoothing 0.10.1. COVID-19 and ISIC use inverse-square-root class weights. The EyePACS classifier uses class-balanced sampling without loss class weights. All training and evaluation ran on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 (24 GB), CUDA 12.4, PyTorch 2.6, and Python 3.11.

Target-domain recalibration fits and audits HC-ROCP on the 1,464-case APTOS calibration split, with the EyePACS-trained classifier frozen.

Appendix E Complete Baseline Comparison and Statistical Tests

Table  reports the full held-out test comparison averaged over ten calibration-split seeds. All methods use the same frozen probabilities and fixed test observations. Standard baselines and exact ROCP calibrate on each seed’s coverage split; HC-ROCP additionally uses construct and safety splits. The comparisons therefore include the cost of data separation.

For set size, we average the number of returned labels over the fixed test set within each seed, then summarize across the same ten seeds for every set-valued method.

Table  reports the action-only LTT adapter.

Statistical Tests.

We use ten stratified calibration partitions (seeds 20260815–20260824). Two-sided paired tt-tests compare seed-level severe-action-error rate and loss. Holm correction is applied separately within each dataset/metric over the 13 eligible baselines. Identical paired values receive p=1p=1. Tests quantify calibration-partition variation conditional on these fixed data and classifier, not new training runs or independent test cohorts. The ISIC release-solver harm value is 0.47%±0.00%0.47\%\pm 0.00\% because all ten coverage-split recalibrations select the same test action pattern.

Practical Significance.

Before these comparisons, we specified minimum effect sizes of 1 percentage point for harm (the primary δ\delta) and 0.1 for loss. For ISIC’s release solver versus HC-ROCP, the Holm-adjusted values are p=0.0679p=0.0679 for harm and p=0.0171p=0.0171 for loss. The mean loss advantage is 0.05460.0546, below the 0.10.1 minimum-effect threshold.

Reporting.

A baseline receives †\dagger if HC-ROCP is better and ‡\ddagger if the baseline is better, requiring both adjusted p<0.05p<0.05 and the relevant minimum effect size. Coverage is reported descriptively. Absence of a mark does not establish equivalence. Evidence labels and certificate counts are not tested. Tables  and  use the same tests.

Appendix F Protocol Diagnostics and Parameter Sensitivity

Table  compares protocol variants on frozen COVID-19 probabilities. The γ=0\gamma=0 exact-ROCP row uses 1,410 calibration cases to fit β\beta, whereas the full protocol constructs its candidate family on 705 cases and uses separate coverage and safety splits. The change from 4.51%4.51\% to 0.50%0.50\% harm is therefore a protocol-level comparison, not an isolated causal effect of adding γ\gamma.

The fixed-β\beta diagnostics use the full protocol’s construct and safety observations, but change the selection rule. Fitting β\beta at γ=0\gamma=0 and choosing the first γ\gamma meeting the safety-count criterion yields 0.7860.786 test coverage. Taking the largest construct-calibrated β\beta across the grid yields loss 1.4051.405.

Reusing calibration observations changes the selected operating point but produces no high-confidence certificate in this experiment. This empirical outcome does not validate the reuse: independence between construction and certification is a condition of Theorem 1. On ISIC, dropping the subgroup multiplicity factor tightens the SCC upper bound from 21.6%21.6\% to 18.9%18.9\%, still above 5%5\%.

Table  isolates candidate screening by starting from the full M=2394M=2394 family. Using only the construct split, we rank candidates by expected-coverage shortfall, expected-harm excess, and utility, then freeze the top LL before testing. We evaluate prespecified L∈{1,5,10,20,50,100,250,500,1000}L\in\{1,5,10,20,50,100,250,500,1000\} separately, with correction L⁡(1+G)L(1+G); the table shows representative sizes. Smaller families tighten the bounds, but no shortlist certifies at 1%1\%. Even one candidate requires more severe cases than are available under zero errors. Aggressive screening can discard the policy recovered by larger shortlists, exposing a trade-off between candidate quality and multiplicity.

Table  reports the coverage-target sensitivity of the recalibrated candidate family. Each row recalibrates its own candidate family, so the candidate sets need not be nested across targets. The 0.950.95 and 0.990.99 targets select the same (β,γ)(\beta,\gamma) pair. At the looser 0.900.90 target, selection instead returns β=6.17\beta=6.17 and γ=31.6\gamma=31.6, with loss 1.1901.190 rather than 1.0801.080. Thus loss is non-monotone across these separately constructed families.

Count Diagnostic.

The real-data series in Figure (a) uses the already selected COVID-19 policy and subsamples its severe safety cases, then applies an unadjusted single-test harm bound. The diagnostic uses 20 subsamples each at nH=50,100,200n_{H}=50,100,200 and the single full safety sample at nH=366n_{H}=366; all gate-pass rates are zero. Because selection used the same safety data, this is an exploratory count diagnostic, not a fresh certification test or an independent estimate of the complete protocol’s power.

Nested Bootstrap.

For each of 500 repetitions at δ=1%\delta=1\%, we resample the full calibration set’s frozen probability–label pairs with replacement within label strata and independently bootstrap the test pairs without stratification (base seed 20260821). We then redraw the three stratified calibration splits, reconstruct the candidate family, repeat all coverage and harm tests, select a policy, and evaluate it on the resampled test set. COVID-19 and ISIC retain expected-risk labels in 500/500500/500 repetitions each, and EyePACS–APTOS retains its empirical label in 500/500500/500.

Appendix G Simplified False-Certification Simulation

We report a simplified simulation of global false-certification rates under different multiplicity and search assumptions (Figure ). With full correction, the observed rate ranges from 0%0\% to 0.25%0.25\%, below the 5%5\% nominal level. We simulate M=100M=100 candidates with true harm 1.1​δ1.1\delta at δ=1%\delta=1\%, using 400 Monte Carlo repetitions per sample size for each of the three settings. The plotted event is at least one false global-harm claim among the candidates.

Full correction uses η=ε/[M⁡(1+G)]\eta=\varepsilon/[M(1+G)] with ε=0.05\varepsilon=0.05 and G=4G=4. Reduced correction uses η=ε/M\eta=\varepsilon/M. The expanded-search curve tests 25​M25M candidates at the full-correction level computed for MM. Each setting and sample size uses a separate random stream derived from seed 20261108. These settings isolate correction and search-size assumptions in binomial harm tests; the coverage gate and data-dependent policy construction are outside this simulation.

For the complete accounting of M⁡(1+G)M(1+G) tests, replacing the per-test allowance by ε/M\varepsilon/M loosens the union-bound ceiling to ε⁡(1+G)=25%\varepsilon(1+G)=25\%. This is a bound on error probability, rather than a predicted or attained rate.

Appendix H Referral Actions and the Action-Space Gap

Adding referral tests how the action space affects the COVID-19 trade-off. The original actions are no action, antibiotics, quarantine, and additional testing. We append a “refer to human” action with fixed modeled cost cc, classify referral as non-harmful, and rerun the joint protocol on the reference split. Across c∈[0.3,1.0]c\in[0.3,1.0], test loss falls from 1.0801.080 to 0.280.28–0.400.40, while the severe-action-error rate stays at or below 0.50%0.50\% (Table ). Referral volume varies from 22%22\% to 100%100\%: at c=0.3c=0.3, the policy refers every case and has loss 0.3000.300. The harm rate is non-monotone in cc because selection minimizes calibration loss among expected-feasible candidates rather than minimizing test harm.
